job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I leave the flat at 6:45 and drive to a housing site on the edge of Leicester, where I'm a junior site engineer for a mid-sized builder. I check measurements, chase deliveries, walk the site with the foreman and write the daily report in the cabin. I did civil engineering at Loughborough, and my final project was a small footbridge design.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a wall go up that I checked myself. What wears me out is the mud, the early starts and the paperwork on top. I rent a room with two housemates, but my parents run a corner shop twenty minutes away and I eat there most Sundays after temple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that sounds like most things people get excited about. At work I'd carry on as I am. A building goes up because people turn up on time and do the job properly, and no program changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit uneasy, but not about AI. My parents' corner shop makes less every year, because of the supermarkets and the rent on the unit. I help with the books on Sundays, and I think about whether I should send money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: do my site hours, finish my chartered engineer's training diary and save 300 pounds a month. I'd put some of it toward my parents' shop costs if they let me. I'd also keep going to temple and the community lunch, because that's where my people are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but about the shop, not the job. My own work feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop is a worry. What is going on there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop's rent went up by twelve percent in the spring. My father won't say it, but I've seen the books, and we're a year or two from trouble. I'm the one in the family with a real salary, so it falls on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told me you never use AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't needed it and I don't trust it. I like to read the drawings myself and check with the foreman, Mr Okafor. If something goes wrong on a site, nobody accepts the excuse that a computer said so.

I'd carry on, because buildings go up through people doing the job **properly**.
think: I'm a bit **uneasy**, but about my parents' shop, not AI.
The shop's rent rose twelve percent, and I'm the one with a real **salary**.
do: Finish my chartered engineer's **training diary** and keep my site hours.
Save **300 pounds** a month and help with the shop's costs.
Keep going to **temple** and the community lunch.
feel: A little **uneasy**, but about the shop, not my own job.
S0.quote: A building goes up because people turn up on time and do the job properly, and no program changes that.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **family money**: the shop's rent, and her role as the earner.
She mistrusts AI for accountability reasons, not fear of technology.
Faith and community are her support system.

steps.text: Finish the chartered engineer training diary and keep full site hours
Save 300 pounds a month and help with the shop's rent
Keep going to the community lunch after temple

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll hit offices before building sites. At work I'd tell the younger engineers not to rely on a program for anything they can't check themselves. If the program is wrong and I signed the report, I'm the one who answers for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy. The planning and paperwork at the head office will shrink first, and the company might want fewer site engineers if software does the reports. I'm on the ground, so I think I'm safer than the office staff, but not completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new reporting app only as much as the company requires. I'd focus on getting my chartered status and learning more about site safety, because that part needs a person. I'd save 400 pounds a month and not take any risks with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. It feels like clouds over the next field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own job could software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The daily reports and the programme planning. I write about two hours of reports a day, and software could do most of it from my photos. I'd still check it, but it's a big chunk of my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the company will ask of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To use a tablet app and upload photos and measurements. I'd do it, slowly, but I wouldn't love it. My foreman Mr Okafor calls it my homework, because I do it at night.

steps.text: Use the reporting app for daily reports after a training session
Finish chartered status and a site safety supervisor course
Save 400 pounds a month in a plain savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we're not ready, and I'd say it plainly. At work I'd say employers shouldn't drop people without notice. Families can't rebuild their lives in two years, and everyone who runs a company ought to understand that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious. The planning, drawings, scheduling and reports would be machine work within two years, and the company would need a lot fewer of us. Robots for hands-on building come about three years later, so site work would last a bit longer, but I'd see my parents' shop struggle too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as much as I can, 800 pounds a month, and cut out everything but rent and food. I'd ask my family about moving back into the flat above the shop, which would save rent. I'd also keep my head down at work, do the site work well and become the person who can't be spared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight stomach, and a feeling of carrying my parents on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about whether the shop is worth saving, and what they'd do if it closed. I'd offer to help with a small online ordering page, though I'm bad with that sort of thing. We'd probably argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the community at temple?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that families should look after each other, and that we should be ready to share. Temple friends will be in the same boat. I'd start a small fund where members put in a little each month.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and employers shouldn't drop people without notice.
I'd say families can't rebuild their lives in two years.
think: I'd be **anxious**, since planning and reports would be machine work in two years.
Site work lasts about three years longer, but my parents' **shop** would also struggle.
do: Save **800 pounds** a month and cut everything except rent and food.
Ask my family about the flat above the **shop** to save rent.
Become the person who can't be **spared** on site.
feel: **Anxious**: a tight stomach and parents on my back.
S2.quote: Families can't rebuild their lives in two years, and everyone who runs a company ought to understand that.
fieldNote: She carries **parents and shop** as part of her stakes.
Her resistance appears as a request to share the load through family and community.
She proposes a community fund rather than state help.

steps.text: Cut everything except rent and food
Start a small monthly fund with the temple community
Ask my parents about the flat above their shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more time but still fast, and I'd ask the company to plan for its staff. Five years means the people who plan for it will be fine, and the ones who wait for a letter won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy and a little anxious. By 2031 the planning and the reports would be automated, and the company might keep a smaller team of engineers. Site work should last until the robots arrive in 2034, so my field work gives me a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my chartered exam in the first year and a site-safety management qualification in the second. I'd save 500 pounds a month and avoid new debt. I'd also look at starting a small family business with my parents that fits their shop, like a local delivery service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a heavy feeling, but not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them for a clear plan for juniors and some training money. I don't expect they'd do it, but I'd ask. I'd also ask which roles they think will be safe, because I'd rather hear it from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With those years I'd be the one who knows how to check what the new machines build. I'd be the one who signs off safety. I don't love the idea of working next to robots, but I'd rather be the person in charge of them than the one they replace.

I'd ask my employer for a clear **plan** and some training money.
think: I'm **uneasy** and a little anxious; reports would be automated by 2031.
Site work should last until **2034**, so my field work gives me a head start.

Save **500 pounds** a month and avoid new debt.

S3.quote: Five years means the people who plan for it will be fine, and the ones who wait for a letter won't.

steps.text: Pass the chartered engineer exam in the first year
Save 500 pounds a month and avoid new debt

Move toward a site safety manager role by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, and the old advice still holds: work hard, save, look after family. Ten years is long enough to become really good at a trade, and a person who's really good at one thing is hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm. By 32 I'd be a chartered engineer and perhaps a site manager. Robots will reach building sites eventually, around 2039, but someone has to answer for safety. I'd worry more about the shop and my parents' retirement than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, finish my chartered status and save toward a deposit. I'd also help my parents plan what to do with the shop, whether that's selling or handing over to someone. I'd try the software tools as they come into the company, because by then I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade feels like a life, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to marry in my late twenties, and my parents would help find the right person. We'd buy a house in Leicester near family. Technology isn't going to change that for me, but I'd make sure my husband and I both have steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about marriage and children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd also take a small stake in some local business, maybe a building firm. It's old-fashioned, but owning something is a good protection.

I'd say being really good at one trade makes you hard to **replace**.
think: I'm fairly **calm**; by 32 I'd be chartered and perhaps a site manager.
I'd worry more about the shop and my parents' **retirement** than my job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I can work hard for anything, but I can't make two years into twenty for my parents' shop. What would help is advance notice from employers, training paid in work time and support for small family shops in the same trouble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me don't complain, we get on. But getting on needs some notice, and my parents shouldn't pay for decisions made in head offices.

headlineQuote: I can work hard for anything, but I can't make two years into twenty for my parents' shop.
portrait: Iris is **22**, a civil engineering graduate working as a junior site engineer for a Leicester house builder.
She has no debt and good savings, but her parents' corner shop is slipping, so family money is her **real** pressure.
She is traditional, trusts work, faith and community over handouts, and **blames** head-office decisions made without notice.
She is resistant: she never uses AI tools, trusts site work and signatures, and does new software only as **homework**.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because two years cannot protect her parents' shop.
whatWouldHelp: Advance **notice** from employers, paid training in work time and help for small family shops.
